title: Panel handoff sketch — runtime candidate impressions (Tess Huang)
content:
Context:
- Quick capture after loop with Tess Huang (candidate for Senior Runtime Engineer). I was on the final 1.5h deep-dive panel focusing on KV cache handling, batching heuristics, and operational debugging. This is a messy handoff for the broader interview panel and hiring committee: high-level impressions, concrete examples Tess gave, interview questions that need a follow-up, and my recommendation.

Top-line summary (TL;DR):
- Strong practical intuition about production tradeoffs (throughput vs tail latency), good debugging stories, pragmatic about tooling.
- Gaps: limited exposure to distributed autoscaling policies at multi-cluster scale (we probed this), and weaker in CUDA-level performance diagnostics (not unusual for infra-focused engineers).
- My leaning: green-light to move to final hire packet if reference checks corroborate leadership on incident triage + system design. Recommend calibration interview with another SRE-focused engineer to validate autoscaling/ops depth.

Candidate persona notes:
- Background: ex-startup infra team (2-3 years) then mid-size company where they owned runtime for model serving (not model training). Comfortable with Go and Python; some Rust exposure.
- Motivations: wants to own low-latency stacks and make measurable cost improvements. Likes hypothesis-driven optimization.
- Compensation ask: signaled mid-senior level comp band, flexible on equity/level if scope includes ownership of batching/observability efforts.

Concrete strengths (examples they gave):
1) KV cache correctness & eviction story: implemented multi-tenant prefix cache that reduced duplicate decode work by ~18% during peak — explained cache key design, sharding, and a bug where stale KV entries caused hallucinated completions; they added per-tenant cache versioning and short-circuit invalidation to fix it.
2) Batching heuristics: built an adaptive batching controller that tuned max-batch-size based on 95th percentile latency targets; used a sliding-window estimator for arrival rate, and fallbacks to best-effort fixed batching when estimator had insufficient samples.
3) Incident triage: walked through a P0 where GPU memory fragmentation led to OOMs under steady load; they used jemalloc stats + nvml to correlate allocation spikes and landed a config change plus a rolling restart plan.

Weaknesses / risks (observable in the loop):
- Distributed autoscaling: when we asked about cross-region spillover and coordinating scale-down policies, they deferred to product constraints and admitted they hadn't designed cross-cluster coordination logic — their experience was primarily single-region fleets. Risk: needs mentorship for multi-region policies and global fallbacks.
- Low-level perf tools: limited hands-on with CUDA kernel tracing (nsight) and custom kernel selection. They can read perf graphs and reason about hotspots but not dive into writing kernels or doing per-op kernel swaps.

Behavioral / collaboration notes:
- Communication: clear, uses diagrams to explain flow; asked good clarifying questions early in the session.
- Tradeoffs: explicit about cost/latency tradeoffs and when to favor simplification.
- Ownership: gave multiple examples of shepherding features from prototype to rollout with post-mortems.

Mini rubric (my quick scoring; subjective):
- System design (distributed): 4/5
- Debugging & incident response: 5/5
- Low-level perf/kernel work: 2.5/5
- Team fit & communication: 4.5/5
- Production readiness for role: 4/5

Questions that remain / suggested follow-ups:
- Ask-for: a short take-home note from Tess on how they'd design a cross-region fallback policy for capacity-constrained model variants (one page). This will probe their current gap without a full interview.
- Reference check: prioritize a question about lead time on learning CUDA/kernel ops and whether they have proactively upskilled when team needs demanded it.
- Ops calibration: schedule a 30m with SRE lead (Kendall Ruiz) to focus on scaling orchestration, global load shedding, and DB of record for capacity state.

Potential role mapping & ramp plan (sketch):
- First 60 days: onboard to serving-runtime codebase, own one model variant’s batching pipeline and reduce cost-per-token by 8–12% via batching/caching changes.
- 60–180 days: lead an initiative to formalize retry/backoff and cross-region fallback playbooks; partner with product to define SLOs and automation for canary rollouts.
- Long term: owner for runtime perf playbook and a small team of 1–2 engineers.

Interview artifacts / notes that matter for committee:
- Whiteboard drawing they used: adaptive batching controller with two modes (adaptive + fixed). I captured the ASCII sketch in the loop notes (attached in Linear).
- Live code challenge: candidate completed the micro-batching exercise (we asked to implement a token-window aggregator) with good tests; style is pragmatic but some edge-case handling was minimal (race around channel close).

Recommendation (what I would vote):
- Move forward to reference + compensation approval. Strong hire for infra-runtime needs; add a short ops-focused calibration interview before final offer to close the autoscaling multi-cluster gap.

Open flags for committee discussion:
- Leveling: Is this a Senior or Staff-level hire? My lean: Senior with Staff potential once they demonstrate cross-region coordination ownership.
- Team placement: Serve on Serving Runtime core for 3–6 months then consider rotation to Dedicated capacity team for broader scaling exposure.

Notes-to-self / action items:
- Request Tess writeup on cross-region fallback (due in 3 business days).
- Book 30m with Kendall Ruiz (SRE) for ops calibration.
- Add reference questions to recruiter thread: focus on CUDA upskilling, cross-region experience, leadership during incidents.

Rough timestamped capture of salient quotes from the loop:
- "We prioritized a short cache TTL per tenant because invalidation complexity grew faster than performance wins." — indicates pragmatic cost-benefit thinking.
- "I’d rather add more observability than more magic heuristics." — good signal for our culture.

Random scratch ideas (brain dump):
- If hired, small onboarding exercise: give them a perf dashboard + a stale-test orchestrator and ask for a 2-week plan to improve 95p latency. Good way to validate impact early.
- Consider pairing them with an ML infra engineer for 1 month to accelerate kernel-level understanding.

End of note.

(If anyone wants raw loop logs or the small test harness, ping me and I’ll attach the run outputs. This doc will be converted to the panel summary doc if we move forward.)
